title: AWS Introduces Enhanced Custom Event Buses for EventBridge
gist: AWS relaunched the EventBridge custom event bus as a shared, organization-wide resource with ordered delivery, replay, deduplication and a new publisher/subscriber throughput pricing model, aimed at the cost and complexity of chaining buses across accounts. Reactions cited are positive, with a Kafka comparison and a note that about 18 cents per GB ingested is high but not unreasonable.

themes.theme: Why AWS relaunched the custom event bus

insights.claim: Multi-account EventBridge users were chaining several interconnected buses, which raised routing costs and operational complexity and made subscriptions and features like ordering harder to manage.
insights.speaker: Micah Walter
insights.so_what: AWS is conceding that its own multi-account pattern was a cost and complexity trap, creating a migration pull toward the new resource.
insights.locator: EventBridge is a managed event bus service

insights.claim: AWS says the workaround of bus-to-bus chaining makes cross-account and bus-to-bus routing charges compound quickly and leaves platform teams without visibility into who subscribes to which events.
insights.speaker: Micah Walter
insights.so_what: Hidden compounding routing fees were a real cost line for heavy EventBridge users; consolidation could cut them.
insights.quote: Platform teams lose visibility into who is subscribing to which events, cross-account and bus-to-bus routing charges compound quickly

insights.claim: Teams needing event ordering were previously forced to build complex workarounds or adopt entirely different technologies, which implies EventBridge was losing such workloads to other products.
insights.speaker: Micah Walter
insights.so_what: Ordered delivery is aimed at recapturing workloads that had gone to streaming or messaging alternatives.
insights.quote: teams that need capabilities like event ordering are forced to build complex workarounds or adopt entirely different technologies

insights.claim: AWS describes the launch as a ground-up relaunch of the original custom event bus resource, because early 2019 design decisions were hard to evolve.
insights.speaker: Jamie Dool
insights.so_what: A new architecture rather than a patch suggests AWS sees event-driven infrastructure as strategic enough to rebuild.
insights.quote: we relaunch the original custom event bus resource

insights.claim: AWS's product manager calls this the biggest EventBridge launch since the service was introduced in July 2019.
insights.speaker: Jamie Dool
insights.so_what: Marks a rare major reset of a seven-year-old core service.
insights.quote: the biggest EventBridge launch since the service introduction in July 2019

insights.claim: The enhanced bus offers a shared organization-wide bus with cross-account publishing and subscriptions, ordered delivery, event replay, content-based deduplication, JSONata transformation, and Avro and Protobuf payload support.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: The feature list moves EventBridge toward streaming-platform territory, overlapping with Kafka-style use cases.
insights.locator: The enhanced EventBridge custom event bus provides

insights.claim: A new Subscriber resource bundles filtering, targets, retries and dead-letter handling into a single object.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Simplifying subscriber management addresses the platform-team visibility problem directly.

insights.claim: Existing custom event buses remain unchanged and enhanced buses are a new resource, so adoption requires opting in rather than an automatic upgrade.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Migration friction and a long tail of legacy buses mean revenue impact will phase in gradually.
insights.quote: Existing custom event buses remain unchanged
insights.locator: Enhanced custom event buses use ingress

insights.claim: Pricing moves to ingress and egress throughput, with publishers charged for ingested events and subscribers charged for delivered events, separating publisher and subscriber costs.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Charging both sides of the bus can shift costs across internal teams and change chargeback dynamics.
insights.quote: publishers charged for ingested events and subscribers for delivered events
insights.locator: Enhanced custom event buses use ingress

insights.claim: Corey Quinn says the roughly 18 cents per GB ingested is hefty but not unreasonable unless doing something profoundly weird with EventBridge.
insights.speaker: Corey Quinn
insights.so_what: A cloud-cost specialist judging the price tolerable suggests limited pushback, though per-GB pricing could bite high-volume users.
insights.quote: It's high, but not unreasonable unless you're doing something profoundly weird with EventBridge.

insights.claim: Quinn objects to positioning the product as being for enterprise, noting that his own AWS estate stands to benefit greatly and that the pricing is not particularly enterprise.
insights.speaker: Corey Quinn
insights.so_what: Enterprise-only framing may understate the addressable base among smaller AWS estates.
insights.quote: only marred by its positioning as "being for enterprise."

insights.claim: The community reaction is described as overwhelmingly positive, with praise split between the simplified architecture and the new features.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Early sentiment is favorable, though this is the author's characterization of reactions.
insights.quote: The community reaction has been overwhelmingly positive

insights.claim: Gregor Hohpe compares the enhanced bus to Kafka, saying it is almost like Kafka but a big step ahead, apart from the naming.
insights.speaker: Gregor Hohpe
insights.so_what: An influential architect likening it to Kafka signals AWS's managed bus now competes for streaming-style workloads.
insights.quote: Almost like Kafka but big step ahead
